column2: Written contract signed by both parties
column3: Verbal agreements are unenforceable. Get every detail in writing before any work begins.

column2: Scope of work is clearly defined
column3: The contract must specify exactly what is and is not included: materials, finishes, brand names, quantities.
Never pay 100% upfront. Common structure: 10–30% down, progress payments tied to milestones, 10% retainage at completion.
Any change to scope, materials, or cost must go through a signed change order. Define this in the contract.

column2: Start date and completion date are listed
column3: Vague timelines lead to delays. Get specific dates. Include a penalty clause for excessive delays if possible.
Who will pull and pay for permits? The contractor should pull permits in their own name — not yours.
Know who else will be working in your home. The contract should name or describe any subcontractors.
What is covered and for how long? Labor warranty minimum: 1 year. Get it in writing with contact info for claims.
You should hold the COI directly. Do not accept contractor's word — get the document and verify it.
Confirm that the contractor will provide lien waivers from subcontractors upon project completion to protect your title.
